senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a founder of a class of priests
to direct or guide the movement of an object, without special regard to point of departure or goal
senses.comment: The Spirit of God is also regarded as an agent in leading or directing the movement of a person, for example, ἤγετο ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ he was led by the Spirit into the desert (Luke 4:1).|ἄγω[a] also occurs in contexts in which the leading involves force: ὅταν ἄγωσιν ὑμᾶς παραδιδόντες whenever you are taken into custody and turned over to the courts (Mark 13:11); Ἤγοντο δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι κακοῦργοι δύο σὺν αὐτῷ ἀναιρεθῆναι they led two others off also, both of them criminals, to be put to death with him (Luke 23:32).

senses.def: to carry or bring, especially animate beings
to move away from a reference point
senses.comment: It would also be possible to translate ἄγωμεν in John 11:7 as let us depart for.

senses.def: to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
senses.comment: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.

senses.def: to be actively performing some function
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘the courts are functioning’ is ‘the courts are open’ or ‘the judges are on duty’ or ‘the officials are listening to complaints.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: to occur at a particular or expected time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἄγω in Luke 24:21, see 67.79.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: to experience a duration of time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἄγω in Luke 24:21, see 67.64.

senses.def: prompter of attention, which serves also to emphasize the following statement
to speak of the excellence of a person, object, or event
senses.comment: In a number of languages praise can only be expressed by direct discourse, and this requires some content which provides the basis for praise. For example, in Luke 2:13 instead of a literal rendering of ‘praising God,’ it may be necessary to have ‘they said, God is wonderful,’ and in Luke 16:8 it may be necessary to translate ‘the master of this dishonest manager said, You are remarkable for having done such a clever thing.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a state of being uncircumcised by not having the foreskin of the penis cut off

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a collective for those who are uncircumcised
senses.comment: In translating Galatians 2:7 it is essential in some languages to avoid the impression that there are two gospels, one for the Jews and another for the Gentiles. One may, therefore, render Galatians 2:7 as ‘I had been entrusted with the good news to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised’ or even ‘God had given me and Peter the task of preaching the good news; I to the Gentiles and Peter to the Jews.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: that which someone has done in violating the will and law of God
to hand over or to deliver to (especially in reference to letters), with the possible implication of a somewhat formal activity
to groan or to sigh deeply or intensely
the state of being devoid of understanding
senses.comment: ἄνοια does not imply in 2 Timothy 3:9 that people are incapable of understanding, but that they evidently are unwilling to understand.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of such extreme anger as to suggest an incapacity to use one’s mind
to cause one’s own death by hanging

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: pertaining to that which is pleasing in view of its being acceptable
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to restructure expressions containing ‘acceptable to’ or ‘pleasing to.’ For example, in Acts 10:35 it may be necessary to translate ‘God accepts whoever worships him and does what is right’ or ‘God is pleased with whoever worships him and does what is right.’ Similarly, in 1 Timothy 2:3 one may translate ‘this is good, and God our Savior likes it’ or ‘… is happy because of it.’

senses.def: to question someone with hostile intent
open vehicle with two or four wheels; harnessed to and pulled by horses; used in war or for travelling
senses.comment: In Revelation 9:9 the reference is to war chariots drawn by horses, while in Acts 8:28 the reference is to a travelling chariot in which the Ethiopian official was riding. In languages which have no technical term for chariot, it is possible to speak of a war chariot as ‘a war carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn cart for fighting.’ A travelling chariot may be described as ‘a travelling carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn vehicle.’ A further description of such chariots may be given in a glossary.

senses.def: a bag made of skin or leather; used for temporarily storing and carrying wine
senses.comment: A number of translators have attempted to substitute ‘bottles’ for ‘wineskins,’ but this has not been satisfactory, since fermenting wine does not normally break glass bottles, while it would break old wineskins. In circumstances in which the use of wineskins is not known, it may be necessary to employ some type of descriptive phrase (for example, ‘a container made of skin’ or ‘a closed bag of skin’ or ‘a goat skin like a bottle’) and a fuller explanation in the margin.

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: pertaining to one who is condemned as the result of his own actions
a king of Moab involved with Balaam
a relatively small number of objects or events, probably implying less than expected
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of a small or limited number of objects is expressed by a negative attribution to an expression of large quantity, so that ‘few’ becomes ‘not many.’ For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in Hebrews 13:22, see 67.106.

senses.def: a relatively small quantity or extent, probably implying less than expected
senses.comment: For βραχύ τι in Hebrews 2:7, see 78.43.

senses.def: a degree of indefinite approximation
senses.comment: In Hebrews 2:7 (a quotation from Psalm 8.6) the expression βραχύ τι as a lexical unit refers to rank. However, Hebrews 2:8 suggests that the writer of Hebrews probably interpreted βραχύ as meaning a small quantity (see 59.14) and as referring to time in the sense of ‘a little (while).’ For this interpretation of τι, see 92.12.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time
senses.comment: In Hebrews 13:22 the phrase διὰ βραχέων may refer to the act of sending the communication or the amount of time required to receive the communication, that is to say, to read the communication or to hear it read. For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in Hebrews 13:22, see 59.4.

senses.def: (derivative of γεννάω[b] ‘to give birth,’ 23.52) pertaining to having been born
senses.comment: In some languages a literal rendering of γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν ‘born of women’ could be misleading, for it might suggest that there are persons who have not been born of women. It is for that reason that γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν may be rendered in some instances as ‘of all those persons who have ever lived.’ However, this reference to the preeminence of John the Baptist is difficult, and the implications of it go far beyond the matter of translational equivalence.

senses.def: to weep, with the clear implication of shedding tears
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between weeping which results from sorrow and grief and weeping caused by physical suffering. Without careful attention to such a distinction, a translator may seriously distort the meaning of the text.

senses.def: second in a series involving either time, space, or set

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a subsequent event, but not necessarily the second in a series
to cause something to be open (see also discussion at 79.111)
to explain something which has been previously hidden or obscure
(idioms, literally: to open the mind, and: to open the heart) to cause someone to be willing to learn and evaluate fairly
glosses: to cause someone to be open-minded
senses.comment: It is rare that one can speak literally of ‘opening the mind’ or ‘opening the heart.’ It is sometimes possible to use an expression such as ‘to cause the mind to see’ or ‘to cause the heart to know’ or ‘… to recognize.’ In some languages, however, ‘to open the mind’ or ‘to open the heart’ may refer to murderous violence.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to open a womb) to be the first offspring of a female
a discourse consisting of an orderly exposition or narration
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to represent the meaning of διήγησις by qualifying the type of writing, for example, ‘many have undertaken to write carefully about what has taken place among us.’ Other equivalent expressions might be ‘to write in detail.’

senses.def: (derivative of δίδωμι[a] ‘to give,’ 57.71) the one who gives
to cause something to go into effect, with the implication of something being newly established
to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
(idiom, literally: to go in and to go out) to live or to conduct oneself in relationship to some community or group
senses.comment: The semantic focus of this idiom in Acts 9:28 appears to be the manner in which a person conducts himself in relationship to others, but it is possible to imply a certain amount of movement. For example, in Acts 9:28 one could translate ‘Paul stayed with them and went about in Jerusalem.’

senses.def: pertaining to being willing to do something without being forced or pressured
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘willingness’ to perform some action is expressed negatively, for example, ‘not having to’ or ‘not being forced to’ or ‘not being told one must.’ A positive expression of ‘willingness’ may be indicated idiomatically by a phrase such as ‘my heart approves.’

senses.def: the state of being free
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of freedom is expressed as a negation of control or domination, for example, ‘where the Spirit of the Lord is present, there is no longer domination’ or ‘… a person is not dominated’ or ‘… a person does not feel under constraint.’

senses.def: a position defined as being within certain limits
senses.comment: Some translations render Mark 5:3 as ‘he lived among the graves,’ but it is likely that the Greek expression refers to living within relatively elaborate tombs.|In Mark 2:8 it is also possible to understand the phrase ἐν ἑαυτοῖς as meaning ‘among themselves’ (see ἐν[b], 83.9).|It may not be possible in some languages to speak of a part of a document as being ‘in’ something. It may, therefore, be necessary to render this expression in 1 Corinthians 5:9 as ‘part of what I wrote to you about was …’

senses.def: a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects

senses.subdomain: On, Upon, On the Surface Of
senses.def: a position on the surface of an area
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be quite impossible to speak of ‘tablets of the human heart’ (2 Corinthians 3:3). An equivalent may be ‘in the human heart’ or ‘in people’s hearts.’ In some languages, however, it may be necessary to substitute ‘mind,’ for example, ‘in people’s minds.’

senses.def: a position in proximity to or in the immediate vicinity of an object or other position
a marker of a state or condition
extension toward a goal which is inside an area
senses.comment: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ἄγγελος γὰρ κυρίου κατὰ καιρὸν κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ ‘an angel of the Lord from time to time went down into the pool’ John 5:3 (apparatus).

senses.def: a marker of close personal association
a marker of attendant circumstances, often with the implication of means
(with the dative) a marker of an immediate instrument
a marker of the manner in which an event occurs
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to restructure this statement in Romans 12:8 and translate ‘one should be generous in sharing with others.’

senses.def: a marker of an area of activity which bears some relation to something else
a marker of that of which something consists
a marker of an experiencer of an event
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret the relation expressed by ἐν in Galatians 1:16 as indicating agent or instrument, for example, ‘to reveal his Son by me’ or ‘… through my life’ (compare ἐν as an expression of agent in 90.6 and instrument in 90.10), or even means (ἐν ἐμοί referring to his behavior) as in 89.76.

senses.subdomain: Agent, Personal or Nonpersonal, Causative or Immediate, Direct or Indirect
senses.def: (with the dative) a marker of agent, often with the implication of an agent being used as an instrument, and in some instances relating to general behavior rather than to some specific event
a marker of objects which serve as symbolic substitutes for supernatural persons or powers presumed to act as guarantors of compliance with oaths
(with the dative) a marker of the means by which one event makes another event possible
a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon instrumentality, either of objects or events
a marker of result, with the probable implication of a preceding process
senses.comment: In some languages this expression in Luke 1:17 may be rendered as ‘to cause the disobedient people to think like the righteous.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a marker of a point of time which is simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: a marker of the extent of time within a unit
(with the dative) a marker of content as a means of specifying a particular referent
(an idiom: in truth) pertaining to being a real or actual event or state
(an idiom, literally: to be in weight, see 86.1) to insist on one’s importance or worth
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret ἐν βάρει εἰμί as denoting a person’s status, and accordingly, one could classify this idiom in Domain 87 Status, but it is also possible to interpret this expression in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 as the demands which could be placed upon persons, and therefore one could translate as ‘we could have made demands on you.’ Such a translation would imply the relationship of authority, and the meaning could be classified in Domain 37 Control, Rule.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have in the womb) to be in a state of pregnancy
senses.comment: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω[b], 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.|It is impossible to determine whether in Matthew 1:23 (ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν ‘she will be pregnant and bear a son’) the focus is upon the state of pregnancy or the fact of conception (see 23.49).

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in great) pertaining to a relatively long duration of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: ἐν ὀλίγῳ - pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐν ὀλίγῳ in Acts 26:28 as meaning ‘easily’ or ‘without difficulty’ (see 22.41).

senses.def: pertaining to that which is accomplished easily or without difficulty
senses.comment: For another, more probable, interpretation of ἐν ὀλίγῳ in Acts 26:28, see 67.106.

senses.def: pertaining to expressions which are not to be understood literally, but symbolically or figuratively
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be more satisfactory to translate ἐν παραβολῇ and πνευματικῶς[c] by a negative expression, for example, ‘not literally’ or ‘not really.’ The expression in Revelation 11:8 might be translated as ‘that city might be called Sodom, but it isn’t really Sodom.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in boldness) in an evident or publicly known manner

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the blinking of an eye) an extremely short duration of time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of the phrase ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, see 16.5.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: a very brief period of time
glosses: quickly (in combination with the preposition ἐν)
senses.comment: In Acts 22:18 τάχος evidently refers to a brief period of time before fulfilling the admonition to leave Jerusalem.

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the darkness) pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the next) a point of time subsequent to another point of time, but with the implication of an ordered sequence

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the hidden) pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the between) an extent of time within another unit or extension of time
(an idiom, literally: in the light) pertaining to being widely known in view of the events in question having taken place in public

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
pertaining to being of considerable value or worth

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: pertaining to high status, involving both honor and respect
the right to control or govern over
the domain or sphere over which one has authority to control or rule
a means or instrument by which authority is marked or symbolized
senses.comment: This passage, however, is subject to a number of different interpretations, as commentaries clearly indicate.

senses.def: one who has the authority to rule or govern
a state of control over someone or something
the power to do something, with or without an added implication of authority
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἐξουσία in Mark 3:15 as meaning ‘authority,’ and in a number of instances it is difficult to determine whether the focus is upon the power which an individual has or a granted authority to do something which naturally implies strength or power (see 37.35 - 37.38).

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of Ephesians 1:21 some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: the right to judge on the basis of having the potential to evaluate
to move to or on to, generally with the implication of having arrived
to move up onto some object
senses.comment: In a high percentage of languages it is necessary to use quite distinct terms in speaking of boarding a ship in contrast with mounting a donkey. A wrong choice in such a context can be seriously misleading.

senses.def: to move to or on to, generally with the implication of having arrived
to attempt to learn something by careful investigation or searching
senses.comment: An equivalent of ‘search’ in the expression ‘search the Scriptures’ may be in some languages simply ‘read carefully’ or ‘study well.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: doing that which is good and beneficial to someone
pertaining to being thankful for what has been done to or for someone
senses.comment: Expressions for ‘thankfulness’ are frequently idiomatic, for example, ‘to have a full heart’ or ‘to speak from the heart’ or even ‘to say, You are very kind.’ For another interpretation of εὐχάριστος in Colossians 3:15, see 33.352.

senses.def: (derivative of εὐχαριστέω[a] ‘to thank,’ 33.349) pertaining to expressing thanks
senses.comment: For another interpretation of εὐχάριστος in Colossians 3:15, see 25.99.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time preceding another point of time and implying completion
senses.comment: Note that the subsequent point of time in Luke 11:7 and Matthew 3:10 is the act of speaking.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: already sometime) a time simultaneous with the discourse but in relationship to preceding time
(derivative of θεός[a] ‘God,’ 12.1) the nature or state of being God
senses.comment: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In Romans 1:20 ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In 2 Peter 1:4 ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

senses.def: any aromatic substance (usually a resin) burned for its pleasing aroma
senses.comment: Since some form of incense is almost universal, there is normally no difficulty involved in finding some term to designate ‘incense.’ However, it is always possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘a substance which gives off a sweet-smelling smoke’ or ‘… a good-smelling smoke.’

senses.def: to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἐλεάω ‘to show mercy,’ 88.76) pertaining to showing mercy

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: mercy to you) a highly elliptical expression equivalent in meaning to the statement may God be merciful to you in sparing you from having to undergo some experience
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
act of causing harm or injury to someone or something (a highly generic meaning involving a wide range of harm and injury)
senses.comment: In translating terms meaning ‘to harm’ or ‘to injure,’ it may be necessary to specify suffering, for example, ‘to cause people to suffer’ or ‘to cause people to have pain.’|In some languages it may be necessary to translate this expression in Acts 7:34 as passive, for example, ‘I have seen the harm done to my people in Egypt’ or, in the active form, ‘I have seen how the people in Egypt harmed my people.’

senses.def: to boast about something by downgrading something else
senses.comment: In many languages it may not be possible to use an expression such as ‘to boast against.’ Therefore, in rendering μὴ κατακαυχῶ τῶν κλάδων in Romans 11:18 one may use ‘you must not say that you are so much better than the branches.’ For another interpretation of κατακαυχάομαι in Romans 11:18, see 88.194.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to despise, with the implication of regarding oneself as superior
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κατακαυχάομαι in Romans 11:18, see 33.370.

senses.def: to have greater power or potential than
senses.comment: The reference to ‘mercy’ and ‘judgment’ in James 2:13 must be related to God’s mercy and judgment.|In a number of languages it is not possible to personify mercy and judgment, and therefore one must relate these two expressions to God, for example, ‘the extent to which God shows mercy is even more than the way in which he judges’ or ‘God shows mercy even more than he judges.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to exploit by means of craftiness and cunning, implying false arguments
glosses: to take advantage of in a cunning manner
senses.comment: It is also possible to render κατασοφίζομαι in Acts 7:19 as ‘to take advantage of by clever words’ or ‘to persuade by sweet talk.’

senses.def: a seaport of the city of Corinth
to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
act of engaging in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
a state characterized by troubling circumstances
(derivative of κτάομαι ‘to acquire,’ 57.58) one who owns or possesses property
to shape rock by cutting, either internally or externally
senses.comment: In some languages important distinctions are made in terms for cutting rock depending upon the type of activity, for example, shaping of rock by cutting, the quarrying of rock from an outcrop, or the hewing of an area inside of an outcropping of rock (a cave-like structure hewn into rock).

senses.def: speaking in a highly insulting manner

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively long duration of time
a sweet substance produced by bees from flower nectar
senses.comment: Though honey may be regarded by some as a vegetable product, since flowers constitute its source, it is more specifically associated with bees and in some languages is actually called bee urine.|μέλι ἄγριον, literally ‘wild honey,’ refers to bee honey gathered in the fields and not the result of keeping bees in hives.|In the ancient world bee keeping was a highly developed industry, since honey was a principal source of sweetening. The equivalent of wild honey in a number of languages is ‘forest honey’ or ‘tree honey.’

senses.def: to determine the measurement of something
senses.comment: In some languages one may best translate this expression in Revelation 21:16 as ‘the angel learned how big the city was’ or, as in other languages, ‘the angel walked the size of the city.’

senses.def: to give a measured portion to someone
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret this expression in Mark 4:24 (and also in Matthew 7:2) as used in a more figurative sense, for example, ‘he will deal with you in the manner that you deal with others.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: sexual intercourse of a man with a married woman other than his own spouse
senses.comment: From the standpoint of the NT, adultery was normally defined in terms of the married status of the woman involved in any such act. In other words, sexual intercourse of a married man with an unmarried woman would usually be regarded as πορνεία ‘fornication’ (88.271), but sexual intercourse of either an unmarried or a married man with someone else’s wife was regarded as adultery, both on the part of the man as well as the woman. In view of the married status of the woman being the determining factor in μοιχάω, μοιχεύω, μοιχάομαι, μοιχεία, and related terms (88.277-88.278), there is a significant contrast with πορνεύω and related expressions (88.271). πορνεύω, however, may be regarded as more generic in meaning, and thus in certain contexts including adultery.

senses.def: to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief
to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action
one who is in charge of running a household
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to indicate that οἰκονόμος[a] was a person hired to engage in a particular activity, and therefore in Luke 16:1 it may be necessary to say ‘there was a rich man who had hired a man to manage his household.’

senses.def: one who has the authority and responsibility for something
glosses: one who is in charge of

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: manager of a city) one who is in charge of the finances of a city
(derivative of ὄνος ‘donkey,’ 4.31) pertaining to a donkey
senses.comment: In rendering Matthew 18:6 it is important to avoid the impression that a donkey would turn the millstone in the same way that a person would. Sometimes a general causative expression may be used, for example, ‘a millstone that a donkey causes to go round (rotate),’ but it may actually be necessary to say ‘… which a donkey causes to go round (rotate) by pulling on a shaft.’ In fact, a marginal note may be necessary in order to avoid serious misunderstanding and to emphasize the fact that such a millstone was large and heavy.

senses.def: pertaining to being made of baked clay
to engage in an activity for the sake of amusement and/or recreation
senses.comment: The specific reference of παίζω in 1 Corinthians 10:7 is probably to dancing, but some scholars interpret παίζω in this context as a euphemism for sex.

senses.def: a change or variation in the nature or character of something
to be very much like something

senses.subdomain: Opposite, Over Against, Across From, Offshore From
senses.def: a position opposite another position, with something intervening
any kind of bird, wild or domestic
senses.comment: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: birds of the sky) wild birds in contrast with domesticated birds such as chickens
senses.comment: A literal rendering of πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, either as ‘birds of the air’ or ‘birds of the sky,’ may be misleading, since ‘birds of the air’ might imply that these are birds made out of air, and ‘birds of the sky’ might suggest they are birds which remain always in the sky. In some languages the equivalent expression is ‘birds of the trees’ or ‘birds of the winds.’

senses.def: to be completely certain of the truth of something
senses.comment: The phrase ‘with complete certainty’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘you may surely believe it’ or ‘there is no reason at all for you to doubt.’

senses.def: a means of gaining a profit or wealth
senses.comment: πορισμός occurs in 1 Timothy 6:6 with an extended meaning of advantage or benefit, but the context shows clearly that this is a rather unusual and perhaps somewhat forced extension of meaning.

senses.def: to know about something prior to some temporal reference point, for example, to know about an event before it happens
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand προγινώσκω in 1 Peter 1:20 as meaning ‘chosen beforehand’ (see 30.100).

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose or select in advance of some other event
senses.comment: In Romans 8:29 προγινώσκω may also be understood as meaning ‘to know beforehand’ (28.6).

senses.def: to accept a message for oneself and to act accordingly
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
to remain in a place and/or state, with expectancy concerning a future event

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to pretend to be engaged in a particular activity
what is said in defense of a particular action, but without real justification
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to have no excuse’ is rendered as ‘to not be able to justify’ or ‘to not be able to give a good reason for.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πωρόω ‘to harden,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause someone to be completely unwilling to learn and to accept new information
glosses: to cause to be completely unwilling to learn
to cause the mind to be closed
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 3:14 and in John 12:40 νόημα and καρδία function syntactically as so-called ‘accusatives of specification.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: the seventh or last day of the week (religiously the most important since it was consecrated to the worship of God)

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: a period of seven days
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to render Luke 18:12 as simply ‘for every seven days, I fast two days.’ For the expression ‘the first day of the week,’ there may be a number of complications, especially since in present-day usage Monday is often regarded as ‘the first day of the week.’ For the NT, of course, the Sabbath Day, or ‘Saturday,’ marked the seventh day of the week and the next day would be regarded as ‘the first day of the week,’ namely, Sunday.

senses.def: a Sabbath day’s journey, somewhat over half a mile and about one kilometer

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: behavior which is befitting, implying a measure of dignity leading to respect
senses.comment: In some languages ‘propriety’ is best expressed as ‘to act in the right way’ or ‘to act as one ought.’

senses.def: a sharp projection of a woody plant (though possibly a splinter of wood) with the implication of its causing injury and discomfort
senses.comment: In the NT σκόλοψ occurs only in the figurative expression σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί ‘thorn in the flesh,’ and this expression has been subject to a number of different interpretations (see 22.20).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: thorn in the flesh) something which causes serious trouble and difficulty
senses.comment: There are a number of different interpretations of σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί in 2 Corinthians 12:7 (see discussion at 20.27).

senses.def: act of rising up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands
to engage in intense and emotional expressions of different opinions
the state of existence, with the implication of being in a place or position

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to sit down with someone or to be seated with someone
to be in a place together with others
one who works together with someone else
slaughtering, either of animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
(an idiom, literally: day of slaughter) a time of destructive judgment
senses.comment: The reference of the phrase ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς in James 5:5 is the destructive judgment of God, but it is possible that σφαγῆς should be interpreted in a more literal sense of ‘destruction’ rather than mere condemnation.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a very short extent of time
senses.comment: In John 11:29 ταχύ probably refers to the short period of time between Mary‘s hearing about Jesus and her getting up to go out to meet him. It is, of course, also possible to interpret ταχύ in John 11:29 as referring to the rapidity of Mary‘s movement in getting up and going out to meet Jesus.|Again, in John 13:27 the emphasis is upon the brief period of time before Judas is to do what he had set out to do.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: an interrogative reference to someone or something

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: an interrogative reference to reason
senses.comment: The expression τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (literally ‘what for me and you?’) in John 2:4 is an adage meaning ‘for what reason are you saying or doing this to me?’ In some languages it may be preferable to translate John 2:4 as ‘why do you ask me this?’ In Mark 1:24 one may translate ‘what do you want with us?’

senses.def: a person greeted in Romans 16:12

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: to pour or run out over, either of a liquid or a dry mass

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: the state of loving money or wealth
to be on one’s guard against some eventuality
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a great deal of difference in terminology employed in speaking about guarding an area in order to apprehend someone and guarding a flock of animals for fear of theft from robbers or danger from wild animals.

senses.def: to lead or guide by taking by the hand
glosses: to lead someone by the hand

senses.def: to separate objects by introducing considerable space or isolation
to dissolve the marriage bond
senses.comment: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in 1 Corinthians 7:11 and χωρίζω in 1 Corinthians 7:15 on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

senses.def: to separate from, as the result of motion away from
to cause to be at a distance
